issues.title: Should security claims be in the base JWT for delegates vs delegate_payload
issues.author: GarethCOliver
issues.body:
Current text says to put them in the delegate_payload, to disambiguate from the KbJwt claims and to allow for each payload to differ (e.g. different exp)

From implementing this, it's kinda a pain. Existing JWT and SD-JWT libraries expect the claims to be in the base. Additionally, it means doing at least some amount of processing of the SD-JWT before being able to access the security claims, which isn't ideal. 

The original reason for doing this was encapsulation and flexibility but given the amount of difficulty it adds to actual implementations I'm not convinced it is worthwhile. If we instead put them in the base and just say 'if you want different ones, create different delegate_sd-jwts', which is always an option, if sometimes inconvenient then this is likely a good trade-off.

issues.title: issuer_jwt_hash name
issues.author: GarethCOliver
issues.body: issuer_jwt_hash isn't a great name, as it is really just the preceeding jwt (which may or may not be an issuer jwt). Renaming to providing clarity (e.g. just jwt_hash or binding_jwt_hash or parent_jwt_hash to complement sd_hash may help)

issues.title: Use a collision-resistance TransactionData type
issues.author: GarethCOliver
issues.body: This specification defines a Transaction Data type for performing delegation-as-presentation. The current type, 'delegate' isn't collision resistant. Should update it to either a urn or an r-dns name.

comments.author: TheBlackBit
comments.body:
+1 to this. OpenID4VP 1.0 Section 5.1 recommends collision-resistant names for type values, and an urn or a reverse-DNS name would both work for us.

AP2’s agent_authorization.md also requires type to be exactly "delegate", so its docs will need to change along with the draft. I’ve opened [google-agentic-commerce/AP2#380](https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2/issues/380) for that.

comments.author: ab-makage
comments.body:
+1 to making the transaction data type collision-resistant.

I wonder if it would also be useful to:

1. use a concrete namespace and make the schema version explicit in the type identifier, for example `urn:delegate:org.ietf.oauth:1`; and
2. make the use of `credential_ids` explicit in the delegate transaction data definition/examples, aligning it with the OpenID4VP transaction data structure.

For example:

```json
{
  "type": "urn:delegate:org.ietf.oauth:1",
  "credential_ids": ["credential_query_id"],
  "format": "dSD-JWT+KB",
  "delegate_payload_disclosure": "...",
  "delegate_disclosures": ["..."]
}
```

Here, `org.ietf.oauth` is proposed as a concrete namespace for this specification, and the final segment (`1`) represents the schema version.

The versioned type identifier would make future schema evolution explicit. PaSO takes a similar approach for OpenID4VP transaction data, using a versioned URN structure such as `urn:paso:sca:<domain>:<suffix>:<version>`.

Also, making the use of `credential_ids` explicit would clarify which DCQL Credential Query the delegation transaction data applies to, consistent with the OpenID4VP transaction data model.

Would a naming and structure along these lines make sense?

issues.title: Clarify how availability of revocation information can effect the chain
issues.author: GarethCOliver
issues.body:
From call for adoption: Cliff Singletary@ 

"Section 6 ends in a binary: “If any of the steps fail then the presentation is invalid and processing MUST be aborted.” For chain integrity that is right; nothing in steps 1–5 is fetched. But Section 8.3 defers revocation to “traditional mechanisms,” which do fetch. Once a verifier consults a status source for any link, it needs to distinguish a chain it evaluated and refused from a chain it could not evaluate because the source did not answer, and to record which link’s status was unavailable. Otherwise an outage reads later as a revocation of the delegator."

comments.author: atakedemo
comments.body:
@GarethCOliver 
I draft proposal. Please review it.

```markdown
## Summary

Section 6 closes with a two-valued outcome: "If any of the steps fail then the presentation is invalid and processing MUST be aborted." For the steps it governs that is exactly right. Steps 1-5 split the chain, verify signatures, compare `sd_hash` / `issuer_jwt_hash` digests, and check `typ` — all local computation over bytes already in hand. They are deterministic and total: they always return a definite answer, so two values suffice.

Section 8.3 then permits something with a different shape. "Traditional mechanisms of credential revocation can be used with delegate SD-JWTs" admits an operation that **retrieves state from a third party**, and retrieval has three outcomes, not two: the source says valid, the source says revoked, or the source does not answer.

The document never marks the transition. A Verifier that follows Section 6 and also acts on Section 8.3 has a third outcome with nowhere to put it, and the natural reading — fold it into "the presentation is invalid and processing MUST be aborted" — destroys the distinction that matters most. **A chain refused because a delegator revoked it and a chain that could not be evaluated because a status source was unreachable become the same recorded event.** The second then reads, later, as the first.

This proposal adds one scoping sentence to Section 6 and one subsection to Section 8.3. It defines no claim, changes no serialization, and adds nothing to the wire. It is offered as adoption-call feedback that is addressable after adoption, not as an objection to it.

## The gap

### The two sections describe operations of different kinds

| | Section 6, steps 1-5 | Section 8.3, status checking |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Inputs | the presentation itself | the presentation **and** external state |
| Network | none | required |
| Outcomes | valid / invalid | valid / revoked / **no answer** |
| Determinism | same input, same result, always | depends on reachability at the moment of asking |
| Who is asked | nobody | a different party per component |

The closing sentence of Section 6 is correct for the left column and silently inherited by the right one. Nothing in the document says the binary stops at the section boundary, and nothing gives the third outcome a name.

### The chain makes an edge case into the expected case

Section 8.3 already states the reason: "unlike a traditional Issuer, an individual Holder can not easily distribute revocation information to Verifiers."

That difficulty is not uniform across the chain. A dSD-JWT with *n* delegations presents *n+1* components, and they are signed by different kinds of party:

* the initial SD-JWT, by an **Issuer** — the party the existing revocation ecosystem is built for;
* each KB-SD-JWT, by a **Holder** or a **Delegate Holder** — the parties Section 8.3 says cannot readily publish status at all.

So the components most likely to have an unreachable or absent status source are also the ones added by this specification, and their number grows with the length of the chain. The condition the document leaves undefined is the one its own mechanism makes common. For the agentic purchase in Section 1 — an AI agent proving a Holder authorized it to buy at a particular merchant — the Holder-issued link is precisely the link whose status a Verifier most wants and is least likely to get.

### What a Verifier cannot reconstruct afterwards

The consequence surfaces after the transaction, not during it. A Verifier that records only "presentation rejected" has, at audit, dispute, or incident-review time, no way to answer:

* Did the delegator withdraw the agent's authority, or was the delegator's status endpoint down?
* **Which** component's status was unavailable — the Issuer's, or one of the delegations?
* Was the check even attempted, or skipped under a policy that permits it?

The first question is the one that decides liability in the use case the Introduction motivates. A user disputing an agent-initiated purchase and a service recovering from a status-endpoint outage produce, under the current text, the same record. Reconstruction after the fact is impossible because the information was never distinguished at the point of decision.

### Short `exp` bounds the window, not the ambiguity

Section 8.3 offers short `exp` values and usage-constraining claims as mitigations, and they are good ones: they shrink the interval during which a revocation needs to be discoverable. They do not help here. They reduce how often a Verifier needs to ask; they do nothing about what it concludes when it asks and gets nothing back. The same holds for the case where "the Holder and the Delegate Holder are managed by the same entity" — that removes the distribution problem for deployments it covers, and leaves it for the rest.

Section 8.3's first sentence concedes that some deployments will perform status checks. This proposal is addressed to those, and is inert for deployments that do not.

## Proposed changes

Two edits. Line references are against `draft-gco-oauth-delegate-sd-jwt.md` at `e44c0c1` (447 lines).

### 1. Scope the binary to the steps it governs (Section 6, L290)

Replace:

> If any of the steps fail then the presentation is invalid and processing MUST be aborted. Otherwise the list of processed SD-JWT and Delegate Payloads MAY be passed to the application to be used for their intended purpose.

with:

> If any of the steps above fail then the presentation is invalid and processing MUST be aborted. Otherwise the list of processed SD-JWT and Delegate Payloads MAY be passed to the application to be used for their intended purpose.
>
> The steps in this section are self-contained: they operate only on the presentation and require no retrieval of external state, and therefore always yield a determinate result. Checking the status of any component against an external source is not one of these steps, and its outcomes are not exhausted by the two above; see (#delegate-sd-jwt-revocation).

The substantive addition is "above" in the first sentence, plus a pointer. The paragraph keeps its normative force and stops being read as covering an operation it was never written for.

### 2. Name the third outcome (new subsection under Section 8.3, after L324)

Retain both existing paragraphs of `## Delegate SD-JWT Revocation` unchanged and append:

> ### Indeterminate Status
>
> Verification as defined in (#verification) yields exactly two outcomes because it consults nothing outside the presentation. Status checking does not share that property: a status source may report that a component is valid, report that it has been revoked, or fail to answer. A Verifier that checks the status of any component in the chain therefore has a third outcome to account for, and MUST NOT treat it as equivalent to the second.
>
> A Verifier that cannot obtain the status of a component:
>
> * MUST NOT treat the presentation as having been refused on the basis of that component's status;
> * MUST determine the disposition of the presentation from local policy. That policy SHOULD state whether an indeterminate status is acceptable, and MAY distinguish components by their position in the chain and by the kind of party that signed them;
> * SHOULD record which component's status could not be obtained, identified by its position in the chain, together with the source consulted.
>
> The last point is not bookkeeping. Each component in the chain may name a different status source, and for components signed by a Holder or a Delegate Holder the difficulty described above makes unavailability an expected condition rather than an exceptional one. A Verifier that records only that a presentation was rejected cannot afterwards distinguish a delegation that a delegator revoked from a delegation whose status it was unable to retrieve. In a subsequent dispute those two have opposite meanings.
>
> Neither disposition is safe to adopt by default, and an adversary able to interfere with a status source can reach whichever one policy selects. Treating indeterminate status as acceptable lets such an adversary suppress a revocation that has in fact occurred. Treating it as grounds for rejection lets the same adversary deny service to every delegation issued by the affected party — and, because Holders are the parties least able to operate resilient status infrastructure, that denial is cheapest to mount exactly where this specification adds structure. This document therefore requires the choice to be made explicitly and the affected component to remain identifiable, rather than selecting one.

## What this does not propose

* no new claim, header parameter, `typ` value, or registry entry;
* no change to either serialization, to the chain structure, or to any digest computation;
* no change to Section 6 steps 1-5, or to the two-valued outcome **for those steps**;
* no status mechanism of its own, and no position on which existing mechanism to use — the point is what a Verifier concludes when one of them is silent, whichever it is;
* no requirement that a Verifier check status at all. Deployments relying on short `exp` per Section 8.3 are unaffected;
* no RECOMMENDED default disposition. Section 8.3 is the wrong place to resolve a question whose correct answer is deployment-specific, and resolving it silently is what this proposal exists to prevent.

## Open questions

1. **`SHOULD` or `MUST` on the record.** Recording is local behaviour and IETF specifications are usually reticent about logging, which is why the text above says `SHOULD`. The counter-argument is that the record is the only thing that makes the distinction survive the transaction, so a `SHOULD` may concede most of what the change is for. Author's and WG's call.
2. **Placement.** Security Considerations is proposed because the failure is an integrity-of-interpretation problem, and because it keeps Section 6 normatively untouched beyond one word. It could equally be a short subsection of Section 6, or a new top-level section on status checking. The latter would be the natural home if a future revision specifies a status mechanism for delegations rather than deferring to existing ones.
3. **Terminology.** "Status source" and "indeterminate" are used above without definition. Section 2.2 currently defines no term for either. Adding them is a small edit and makes the requirement citable; omitting them keeps the diff smaller.
4. **Privacy interaction.** A Verifier that consults a per-component status source reveals to each signing party that a presentation involving it occurred, and chain-length-many such lookups leak the shape of the delegation chain to whoever observes them. Section 9 currently defers wholesale to RFC 9901 Section 10, which does not contemplate a chain. This is adjacent rather than part of the above, and is raised in case the author would rather address both at once.

## Relationship to the adoption call

The underlying observation is Cliff Singletary's, made during the call for adoption. This is an attempt to turn it into applicable text rather than to restate it.

It is deliberately scoped so that nothing here needs to be settled before adoption. The change touches one word of normative text and adds one Security Considerations subsection; it does not interact with the format, the verification algorithm, or the IANA registrations the adoption call is really about. Happy to open a pull request against whichever of the placements in open question 2 the author prefers.
```

issues.title: Place requirements, or clarify that constraints can only narrow across the chain
issues.author: GarethCOliver
issues.body: From call for adoption: Cliff Singletary: "Section 8.2 lets an Issuer or Holder put constraints in “visible claims,” but nothing in Section 6 requires the verifier to check that each Delegate Payload stays within the constraints of the link that issued it. Narrowing-only across the chain should be a verifier requirement rather than a policy option, or the chain carries attribution but not bounded authority."

pulls.title: feat-OID4VP-Transaction-Data-type
pulls.author: ab-makage
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR updates the OpenID4VP delegate `transaction_data` definition to use a collision-resistant and versioned type identifier following the pattern:

`urn:delegate:<namespace>:<version>`

It also explicitly documents the use of `type` and `credential_ids` in the delegate transaction data definition and adds a concrete example of the resulting `transaction_data` structure.

## Motivation

The current delegate transaction data type is identified by the value `delegate`.

As discussed in #6, this value is not collision-resistant and could conflict with transaction data types defined by other specifications.

This PR therefore proposes the following type identifier pattern:

`urn:delegate:<namespace>:<version>`

The `<namespace>` segment identifies the namespace of the delegate transaction data type, while `<version>` identifies the schema version.

Including the schema version in the type identifier provides a clear path for future evolution of the delegate transaction data structure, allowing different schema versions to use distinct type identifiers.

This follows a similar versioning approach to PaSO transaction data type identifiers, which use the form:

`urn:paso:sca:<domain>:<suffix>:<version>`

OpenID4VP 1.0 defines `type` and `credential_ids` as parameters of a `transaction_data` object. This PR therefore makes their use explicit in the delegate transaction data definition as well. In particular, `credential_ids` identifies the DCQL Credential Query or Queries to which the delegation transaction data applies.

## Changes

This PR:

- replaces the `delegate` transaction data type with the collision-resistant and versioned pattern `urn:delegate:<namespace>:<version>`;
- explicitly documents `type` as a REQUIRED parameter following the `urn:delegate:<namespace>:<version>` format;
- defines the `<namespace>` segment as identifying the namespace of the delegate transaction data type;
- defines the final `<version>` segment as identifying the delegate transaction data schema version;
- makes the use of `credential_ids` explicit, consistent with the OpenID4VP 1.0 transaction data definition, to identify the DCQL Credential Query or Queries to which the delegate transaction data applies;
- retains the existing delegate-specific parameters:
  - `format`
  - `delegate_payload_disclosure`
  - `delegate_disclosures`
- adds a decoded JSON example of the resulting delegate `transaction_data` structure; and
- updates references to the previous `delegate` transaction data type to use the new type identifier pattern.

## Example

The following is an example using `org.ietf.oauth` as the namespace and `1` as the schema version:

```json
{
  "type": "urn:delegate:org.ietf.oauth:1",
  "credential_ids": ["credential_query_id"],
  "format": "dSD-JWT+KB",
  "delegate_payload_disclosure": "...",
  "delegate_disclosures": ["..."]
}
```

In this example:

- `org.ietf.oauth` is the namespace; and
- `1` is the delegate transaction data schema version.

The `credential_ids` parameter references the applicable DCQL Credential Query identifier or identifiers, making the relationship between the OpenID4VP DCQL query and the delegation transaction data explicit.

## Compatibility

This change does not alter the existing delegate-specific fields or their semantics.

The existing `format`, `delegate_payload_disclosure`, and `delegate_disclosures` parameters are retained.

The primary changes are:

- adoption of the collision-resistant and versioned `urn:delegate:<namespace>:<version>` type identifier pattern;
- explicit documentation of the `type` and `credential_ids` parameters defined by OpenID4VP 1.0;
- explicit definition of the namespace and schema version components of the type identifier; and
- addition of a concrete transaction data example.

## Related Issue

Addresses #6.
